content.text: What is Stock Market?
The stock market is a place where people buy and sell shares of companies. When you buy a share, you are buying a small ownership in that company.
It helps companies raise money and allows investors to grow their wealth over time.
How it Started
The stock market began in the 1600s with the Dutch East India Company. It needed money for global trade operations like transporting spices, silk, and gold.
Instead of taking loans, the company offered shares to the public. Investors received a portion of profits in return.
People started buying and selling these shares in public places like coffee houses, which led to the creation of the first stock market.
How Companies Raise Money (IPO)
When a company wants to grow, it needs money. It can raise this money by selling shares to the public through an Initial Public Offering (IPO).
After the IPO, anyone can buy shares and become a partial owner of the company.
The money collected is used by the company to expand its business and create new opportunities.
How Stock Prices Work
Stock prices are mainly driven by demand and supply. When more people want to buy a stock, its price goes up.
When more people want to sell, the price goes down.
Company performance, news, and investor expectations all influence this demand and supply.
Key Components
Stock/Share: A unit of ownership in a company.
Stock Exchange: A platform like NSE or BSE where buying and selling happens.
Broker: An app or service like Zerodha or Groww that allows you to trade.
Index: A group of top companies representing the market, such as Nifty 50 or Sensex.
Why People Invest
People invest in the stock market to grow their wealth over time.
Historically, the stock market has provided better returns than traditional savings and helps beat inflation.
It also allows individuals to participate in the growth of companies and the economy.
Risks & Reality
The stock market is not risk-free. Prices can go up or down quickly, leading to profits or losses.
Factors like economic changes, company performance, and investor emotions affect stock prices.
Successful investing requires patience, discipline, and a long-term mindset.
Simple Example
Imagine a company sells shares at ₹100 each. You buy 10 shares, investing ₹1000.
If the company grows and the price rises to ₹150, your investment becomes ₹1500.
If you sell at that point, you make a profit of ₹500 (excluding fees).
